2.text: split with the knife; and the “fortifier,” on inspecting them closely, will

3.text: proclaim to the by-standers the probable reason of the death. For instance,

4.text: once in my presence it was said, “The liver is quite diseased, the heart is full

5.text: of pus. With organs in such a state, it was evidently impossible to live any

6.text: longer.” Another time it was said, “The liver looks dry; the heart is

7.text: shrunken to a small lump. It shows that the deceased one died from fear,

8.text: from despair at the attack of the keˊlet.”

9.text: I was told that sometimes indications are found of the harmful influence

10.text: of evil “spells,” created by some human enemy of the deceased; but I had

11.text: no opportunity of witnessing a case like that.

12.text: At last the “fortifier” cuts the throat of the corpse, and leaves the body.

13.text: This last stroke is to prevent the spirit of the deceased from following the

14.text: people of the cortège, and it is considered quite indispensable. A murderer,
14.note: §2.15 withdrawn: printed mark restored, read off the scan

15.text: even, after despatching his victim and before leaving the body, cuts the

16.text: throat, in order to prevent the spirit of the victim from pursuing him. A

17.text: desire to free the soul of the dead, which will escape through the cut and

18.text: fly away with such impetus as to make it difficult for it to come back again,

19.text: is given as the reason for these actions.

20.text: Protecting-Incantations. — After the ceremony is ended, the participants

21.text: arrange themselves again, but the order of the cortège is reversed. It passes
21.note: §2.15 withdrawn: printed mark restored, read off the scan

22.text: now around the body from left to right, and proceeds on its return to the

23.text: camp. The changing of the order is, of course, a defensive measure to ward off

24.text: pursuit by the dead. On the return journey, the “fortifier” and the chief of

25.text: the cortège, who now close the rear, perform several incantations, all of
25.note: §2.15 withdrawn: printed mark restored, read off the scan

26.text: which, so to speak, belong to the cycle of the “magic-flight” tales.

27.text: Thus the chief of the cortège, having with him a snow-beater, now
27.note: §2.15 withdrawn: printed mark restored, read off the scan

28.text: traces with its point at several localities, after the procession has passed by,

29.text: a line across the road. This line is to be transformed into a chasm or into

30.text: a deep river. The “fortifying” person will leave behind one or several small

31.text: stones, which will be turned into steep mountains. He will bring along a

32.text: small cup and the bunch of grass which served for washing the corpse, and

33.text: will hide these objects separately in the snow on his return journey. The

34.text: cup will transform itself into a sea, and the grass into a dense forest.

35.text: Similar incantations are repeated at home, before the entrance of the tent.

36.text: The skins of the slaughtered reindeer are taken to the house and spread

37.text: in the sleeping-room, where they must remain for five days. The “fortifying”

38.text: person enchants a piece of sheet-iron having many holes pierced in it. This

39.text: iron is placed under one of the skins of the bedding in the sleeping-room. If

40.text: the deceased should try to enter the sleeping-room from under ground, he

41.text: would be caught in the holes in the sheet-iron, which would act like an iron net.

42.text: The oldest two women of the tent must meet the cortège on its arrival.
42.note: §2.15 withdrawn: printed mark restored, read off the scan

43.text: They present to the returning people a bunch of newly twisted sinew-thread
